seoDesc: 0-60: work out motor from the engine power and the empty weight. A free everyday life calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the engine power, the empty weight and the payload weight and the 0-60 calculator solves for motor. Think of it as a shortcut for a practical question that turns up in daily life. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the 0-60 calculator work?
sections.html:
The 0-60 calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports motor in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the type of vehicle, the drive type and the gearbox); then you type in the engine power, the empty weight and the payload weight.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the 0-60 calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Motor=100 × (-gearbox + 0-60 time) ÷ ((conditions × tires + 10 × conditions + 10 × tires + 100) × the larger of (conditions + drive type + tires, (8978 ÷ 25) × type of vehicle × (empty weight + payload weight) ÷ engine power))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Engine power = 10 hp(l), Empty weight = 10 kg, Payload weight = 10 kg and Type of vehicle set to Sports car. The calculator returns 0-60 time = 0.299 sec.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: 0-60 time = 0.299 sec should be roughly the size you expected from Engine power = 10 hp(l) and Empty weight = 10 kg.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• The option the calculation settles on.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Power, opening in mechanical horsepowers
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Time, opening in seconds

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The 0-60 calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the engine power, the empty weight and the payload weight — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the 0-60 calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns motor, derived from the engine power, the empty weight and the payload weight. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the 0-60 calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the engine power, the empty weight and the payload weight, which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter engine power in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Engine power opens in mechanical horsepowers and the chip beside it offers 21 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (6 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports 0-60 time = 0.299 sec. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the 0-60 calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
